Chapter 13, the Yoga of the Distinction between the Field and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrakṣetrajñavibhāgayoga), opens a new movement in the poem with no question from Arjuna at all: Kṛṣṇa simply continues speaking, unprompted, from where chapter 12 left off. He introduces by name the classical Sāṃkhya distinction between the field (kṣetra) — the body together with its whole apparatus of matter, senses, and mental states — and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), the conscious self that inhabits and knows it, whom Kṛṣṇa identifies with himself, present as such a knower in every field. He analyzes the field into twenty-four constituents (the five elements, the ego, the intellect, the unmanifest, the eleven senses, and the five sense-objects) together with its further modifications, desire, aversion, pleasure and pain among them, and then defines true knowledge not as doctrine but as a long list of virtues — humility, non-violence, equanimity, unwavering devotion, and constancy in self-knowledge — that culminates in a description of brahman built entirely from paradox: it has hands and feet, eyes and faces on every side, yet is without senses; it is unattached yet sustains everything; it is far away and yet near; it is one, undivided, yet seems divided among the many beings it inhabits. The chapter then turns to nature (prakṛti) and the Person (puruṣa), restating their dualism in Sāṃkhya terms — nature alone is the source of all activity and of the three guṇas, while the Person is merely a witness who becomes entangled only through attachment to what he experiences through nature — and surveys the different roads by which this can be understood: meditation, sāṃkhya, the yoga of action, or simple faith taken on the word of others. It closes with two similes, space and the sun, for how the self remains untouched by, even while illuminating, the body it pervades, and with a final teaching that liberation is nothing other than seeing, with the eye of knowledge, this very distinction between the field and its knower.
